description: We are the Last Minute Challengers, a passionate team assembled for the NASA Space Apps Challenge Raipur. Tackling the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge, our goal is to leverage space agency datasets, terrain mapping, and smart analytics to identify safe, high-priority landing zones on the lunar surface. Though we thrive under pressure, our focus is on building a robust, data-driven solution that supports the next era of lunar exploration.
summary: The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an aerospace mission-planning platform developed to autonomously identify, rank, and evaluate safe 100m × 100m landing parcels across the lunar surface and South Pole.
details:
1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an aerospace mission-planning platform designed to autonomously evaluate, rank, and visualize safe 100m × 100m landing parcels across the Moon, with specialized focus on the challenging lunar South Pole (85−90 degrees).

It operates across a two-part architecture:

  1. Scientific Data Processing Pipeline: Ingests high-resolution NASA LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and queries the NASA JPL Horizons Ephemeris REST API. For every 100m parcel, it computes topographic elevation relative to the lunar radius (RM=1737.4 km), calculates local slopes using finite-difference gradients, and performs 360° raymarching out to 25 km to generate obstacle horizon masks that account for the Moon’s spherical curvature drop.
  2. Interactive Telemetry Console: A high-performance web interface rendering real-time mission controls. Users can scrub through UTC epochs with speed multipliers (1x -168x), examine topocentric solar and Earth line-of-sight angles, review a 14-day continuous power and RF communication window, and inspect landing sites on high-resolution multi-agency basemaps (NASA LROC, USGS, LOLA Color, and ISRO OHRC). Clicking anywhere on the surface dynamically interpolates local slope, elevation, and horizon profile from the nearest high-resolution DEM parcel.

2. What Benefits Does It Have & What Is the Intended Impact?

  • Prevents Catastrophic Lander Tip-Over: Evaluates local slope gradients against strict landing thresholds (≤8° for robotic landers, ≤5° for crewed missions), drastically reducing touchdown hazards.
  • Ensures Uninterrupted Solar Power & Earth Communications: High-relief crater rims at the South Pole cast long shadows that create Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). Our topocentric horizon radar and 14-day ephemeris charts verify line-of-sight margins for direct radio communication and solar array illumination.
  • Accelerates Mission Planning: Automates weeks of manual geospatial and orbital mechanics analysis into instantaneous multi-objective candidate ranking.
  • Cross-Agency Synergy: Bridges datasets from NASA, USGS, and ISRO into a single unified situational-awareness dashboard.

3. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Were Used?

  • Frontend & Web Framework: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons.
  • Cartography & Visualization: Leaflet / React-Leaflet with fractional over-zoom support, HTML5 Canvas (360° topocentric horizon radar), and custom responsive SVG data visualizations.
  • Backend & Data Pipeline: Python 3.9+, NumPy, Rasterio, Tifffile, SciPy, Requests.
    • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) & Goddard Space Flight Center (LOLA DEMs).
    • NASA JPL Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System (REST API).
    • NASA LROC WAC Global Mosaic & USGS Astrogeology Planetary WMS.
    • ISRO ISSDC Chandrayaan-2/3 Dual-Frequency SAR (DFSAR) and Orbiter High Resolution Camera (OHRC) telemetry.
  • AI-Assisted Development: Built with the assistance of Antigravity Google Gemini 3.8 flash, with all code, algorithms, physics calculations, and telemetry thoroughly verified and tested by our team.
  • Platform used for coding: We have used VS Code for building the program

4. How Is the Project Creative?

  • Dynamic 100m Bounding Box Geometry: Accurately accounts for selenographic spherical convergence, widening longitude spans dynamically as latitude approaches the South Pole so the lander target maintains an authentic 100m ground footprint.
  • Interactive 360° Crater Horizon Radar: Rather than treating terrain as a 2D flat plane, the canvas radar projects the true 3D horizon silhouette, showing whether the Sun or Earth is obstructed by distant crater rims.
  • 14-Day Dual-Vector Ephemeris Curve: Visualizes continuous 336-hour trajectories for both solar elevation and direct-to-Earth communication angles simultaneously, giving flight dynamics teams instant insight into upcoming day/night cycles and RF loss-of-signal events.
  • Universal Point Telemetry: Allows mission controllers to click any custom point on the Moon to immediately interpolate real LOLA elevation, slope, and horizon obstruction data on the fly.

5. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • Lander Structural Limits: Dynamic safety profiles tailored to CLPS robotic landers versus Artemis crewed landers.
  • Topographic Shadowing vs. PSR Ice Proximity: Balancing the need for continuous sunlight on solar panels with proximity to permanently shadowed craters containing valuable water-ice volatiles (evaluated via ISRO DFSAR radar confidence).
  • Communication Latency & Line-of-Sight: Direct Earth visibility without relying on relay orbiters.
  • Authentic Planetary Data: Utilizing real lunar altimetry and ephemeris coordinate systems to ensure realistic mission fidelity.
